questions.question: You have 3 red blocks and 4 blue blocks. You count red first: 3 + 4. Your friend counts blue first: 4 + 3. How many blocks does each of you have?
questions.explain: You both have all the blocks, so you both get 7. Swapping the order of adding does not change the total.

questions.question: Your teacher puts 2 red counters and 6 blue counters on the desk. Then she swaps them so 6 blue are first. How many counters are on the desk now?
questions.explain: The counters did not disappear. 2 + 6 = 8 and 6 + 2 = 8. The order of adding does not change the total.

questions.question: Tom knows 4 + 7 = 11. Does that mean 7 + 4 = 11 too?
questions.explain: Yes! If 4 + 7 = 11, then 7 + 4 = 11 as well. Adding in either order always gives the same sum.

questions.question: Jade has 5 red stickers and 3 blue stickers. Her friend says 5 + 3 and 3 + 5 give different answers. Who is right?
questions.explain: Adding in either order gives the same sum. 5 + 3 = 8 and 3 + 5 = 8, so Jade is right.

questions.question: Sam has 10 crackers. He eats 4. His friend says 10 - 4 is the same as 4 - 10. Is his friend right?
questions.explain: Subtraction does not turn around. 10 - 4 = 6, but 4 - 10 does not equal 6. You cannot just swap the numbers.

questions.question: Maya is doing 6 + 2 at home. She gets bored and tries 2 + 6 instead. Will she get a different answer?
questions.explain: Both 6 + 2 and 2 + 6 equal 8. Swapping the order of adding always gives the same sum.

questions.question: Tom has 9 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. He says he can count 9+3 or 3+9 and get the same number. His friend says that only works if the big number is first. Who is right?
questions.explain: Tom is right. 9 + 3 = 12 and 3 + 9 = 12. The order of adding never changes the sum, no matter the numbers.

questions.question: Sam has 7 red dots. He adds 3 blue dots. Then he rewrites it as 3 + 7. How many dots does he have, and is his new equation correct?
questions.explain: 7 + 3 = 10 and 3 + 7 = 10. Both give the same sum, so his equation is correct and he has 10 dots.

questions.question: Maya writes: 8 + 2 = 10. She then writes 2 + 8 = ___. What number goes in the blank, and why?
options: 10, because the sum is the same
questions.explain: 2 + 8 = 10, the same as 8 + 2. The sum does not change when you swap the order of adding.

questions.question: Tom has 9 gummy bears and eats 2. He says 9 - 2 = 7, so 2 - 9 = 7 too, but his friend says that does not work. Who is right?
questions.explain: The friend is right. 9 - 2 = 7, but 2 - 9 is not 7. Subtraction does not turn around like addition does.

questions.question: Ravi and Nina look at a group of 7 crayons and a group of 5 crayons. Ravi adds 7 + 5. Nina adds 5 + 7. What is true?
questions.explain: Adding in either order gives the same sum, so 7 + 5 and 5 + 7 are both 12. The trap is thinking the bigger number has to come first.

questions.question: A class has 12 kids in the red group and 5 kids in the blue group. Which line is true?
questions.explain: Both groups are still there, so 12 + 5 and 5 + 12 are both 17. Taking away does not turn around, because you cannot take 12 kids from 5.

questions.question: A basket holds 9 pinecones. Sara takes 4 out and writes 9 - 4 = 5. Can she also write 4 - 9 = 5?
questions.explain: She started with 9 and took 4 away, so only 9 - 4 = 5 fits. Turning around works for adding, not for taking away.

questions.question: One bag holds 9 red grapes. Another bag holds 6 green grapes. Ben says the total is 15 no matter which bag he counts first. Is he right?
questions.explain: Counting a different bag first moves no grapes, so 9 + 6 and 6 + 9 are both 15. Watch out for thinking the second way gives one more or one less.

questions.question: Mia picks 6 apples, then 8 more. Ben picks 8 apples first, then 6 more. Each of them eats 1 apple. Which is true?
questions.explain: Order does not change a sum, so both picked 14, and 14 - 1 leaves 13 each. The trap is adding the eaten apple instead of taking it away.

questions.question: Leo has 16 stickers. He puts 9 in one pocket and the rest in the other pocket. He writes 9 + ___ = 16. Which is right?
questions.explain: 9 and 7 make 16, and turning it around to 7 + 9 still makes 16. Here you look for the missing part, so do not add 9 and 16 together.

questions.question: Ana has 13 hockey cards. She gives 5 to her cousin. She writes 5 - 13 = 8 and says the order does not matter. What is her mistake?
questions.explain: Ana had 13 and gave 5 away, so only 13 - 5 = 8 tells her story. Adding can be turned around, but taking away cannot.

questions.question: Mr. Lee writes four pairs on the board. Which pair gives the same answer both ways?
questions.explain: Adding turns around, so 8 + 5 and 5 + 8 are both 13. Take-away pairs do not match, and swapping a number for a new one changes the sum too.
